objectives: Trace ballistics from Goddard's 1929 founding through the comparison microscope, IBIS / NIBIN, and modern firearm + tool-mark identification.
Apply rifling + lands + grooves + cartridge-case marking to bullet + casing comparisons.
Recognize the AFTE methodology + the empirical critiques (NAS 2009 + PCAST 2016) of pattern-based firearm identification.

slides.title: Goddard, the comparison microscope, and the birth of ballistics
slides.body:
**Forensic ballistics** examines firearms, ammunition, bullets, cartridge cases, gunshot residue (GSR), wound ballistics, + bullet trajectory. The discipline is one of the older instrumental forensic sciences — predating DNA by half a century — and rests on a single empirical claim: the tool marks left by a firearm on a bullet + cartridge case are sufficient to associate that bullet / casing to a specific firearm (or to exclude it).

**Goddard + the St. Valentine's Day Massacre (1929)**:
- **Calvin Goddard (1891-1955)**: US Army colonel + physician + firearms examiner. With Charles Waite + Philip Gravelle + John Fisher founded the **Bureau of Forensic Ballistics** (NYC, 1925) — first US forensic firearms lab.
- **St. Valentine's Day Massacre (Chicago, Feb 14 1929)**: seven members of the North Side Gang shot dead with Thompson submachine guns. Police suspected Al Capone's South Side gang; Capone denied. Goddard was retained by an independent businessmen's group; he microscopically compared the recovered .45 ACP cartridge cases to test-fires from Tommy guns + ruled out CPD weapons but conclusively matched cases to two Thompsons later found in the possession of Capone gunman Fred Burke (Dec 1929 St. Joseph Michigan arrest). Conviction followed. The case demonstrated the power of microscopic firearms comparison + made Goddard the dominant US firearms expert.
- Goddard's Bureau evolved into the **Northwestern University Scientific Crime Detection Laboratory (1929)** — the first independent US forensic crime lab — eventually folded into Chicago PD then FBI.

**Philip Gravelle's comparison microscope (1925)**: two stages + a single optical bridge + viewing eyepiece. The two specimens are illuminated, rotated, + aligned by the examiner so they appear side-by-side at identical magnification — bullet next to bullet, breech-face mark next to breech-face mark. This single instrument enabled **direct visual comparison of striae** (microscopic linear marks left by rifling + tool surfaces) — the workhorse of firearms identification for a century.

**Modern firearms unit workflow**:
- Receive ammunition + fired bullets + cartridge cases + suspect firearms + crime-scene firearms.
- **Test-fire** suspect firearms into water tank or cotton-bale catcher (preserving bullet without deforming).
- **Microscopic comparison** of test-fires to questioned bullets + casings.
- **Database search** via IBIS / NIBIN (we cover next slide).
- **Trajectory reconstruction** at scene + lab.
- **Distance determination** (muzzle-to-target) from GSR pattern + sooting.
- **Wound ballistics** in collaboration with pathologist.
- **Operability + function testing** (is the weapon mechanically capable of firing?).

slides.title: Rifling, lands and grooves, breech-face marks, IBIS / NIBIN
slides.body:
**Rifling** is the helical pattern of grooves cut or pressed into the interior of a firearm barrel to impart spin to the bullet for stability (gyroscopic stabilization). Rifling is *the* feature that links a bullet to a barrel.

**Rifling characteristics** (class characteristics):
- **Number of lands + grooves** (typically 4-8; Colt = 6 right; S&W = 5 right; Glock = polygonal hexagonal).
- **Direction of twist** (right or left).
- **Twist rate** (one full turn per N inches; e.g. 1:10 in .308 Winchester).
- **Land + groove widths**.
- **Rifling type**: cut (broached), button-rifled, hammer-forged, **polygonal** (Glock, H&K, many modern; no sharp land-groove boundary — produces faint but real striae).

**Individual characteristics**: random tool marks on each barrel (left by manufacturing burrs, broaching tool wear, hand-finishing) produce **microscopic striae** along each land + groove. These reproduce on the bullet's bearing surface as engraved striae. Comparison microscope alignment of striae between questioned + test-fire bullet → identification, exclusion, or inconclusive (per AFTE conclusion tier).

**Cartridge case markings** — from a fired cartridge case:
- **Breech-face impression**: the back of the cartridge case stamped against the breech face when fired (chamber pressure forces case rim against breech). Microscopic breech-face texture (machine-tool marks) imprints into the soft brass.
- **Firing-pin impression**: shape + striae of the firing pin.
- **Ejector mark**: where the ejector lever scrapes the case during extraction.
- **Extractor mark**: on the rim where the extractor claw gripped.
- **Chamber marks**: long striations on the case body from chamber finishing.
- **Magazine marks** + **feed marks** on the case + the bullet.

**AFTE (Association of Firearm + Tool-mark Examiners)** is the international professional society + standards body (founded 1969). **AFTE conclusion tiers**:
- **Identification**: agreement of all discernible class + sufficient individual characteristics; the questioned + known were fired by the same firearm.
- **Inconclusive**: agreement of class characteristics but not sufficient individual; or disagreement of class characteristics ambiguous.
- **Elimination**: disagreement of class characteristics or sufficient individual characteristics.
- **Unsuitable**: not enough discernible characteristics.

**IBIS (Integrated Ballistic Identification System)** — developed by Forensic Technology Inc. (now Ultra Electronics); used internationally. Digital 3D imaging of bullet + cartridge case surfaces; algorithmic similarity scoring; produces ranked candidate list — like AFIS for fingerprints, IBIS gives **leads, not identifications**. Human firearms examiner confirms via comparison microscope on the actual exhibits.

**NIBIN (National Integrated Ballistic Information Network)** — the FBI / ATF US national network of IBIS systems. ATF operates NIBIN; over 4 million entries; thousands of lead-generation hits annually linking unsolved cases. NIBIN hits *initiate* investigations; the actual identification remains a human-examiner ACE-V-style comparison.

slides.title: Tool marks, trajectory, GSR, and the modern critiques
slides.body:
**Tool marks** generalize the ballistics concept beyond firearms — any tool (screwdriver, pry bar, bolt cutter, hammer, knife, drill) leaves striae + impressions on softer materials it contacts. The principles are the same: class characteristics (tool type, width, geometry) + individual characteristics (microscopic striae from tool wear + manufacturing).

**Tool mark types**:
- **Compression / impression marks** (hammer striking, padlock body marks): 2D / 3D shape impressions.
- **Sliding / striated marks** (screwdriver prying a door, wirecutters): linear striae.
- **Cut marks** (knife, saw, bolt cutter): characteristic of the cutting edge.

**Tool-mark comparison**: comparison microscope (Gravelle 1925), same methodology as firearms; AFTE conclusion tiers. Often used to link burglary tools to scenes (pry bar to door jamb), wire-cutter to fence severance, locked-padlock cuts.

**Bullet trajectory reconstruction**:
- **At scene**: bullet path through walls / doors / glass / bodies established by string + laser + photographic + 3D-scan methods.
- **Trajectory rod kits**: rigid rods inserted through bullet holes establish straight-line path; back-azimuth to shooter position.
- **Ricochet analysis** + secondary impacts.
- **Computer modeling** (3D scene scanning + ballistics simulation).
- **Wound ballistics** (with pathologist): entry vs. exit, range, caliber from wound morphology.

**Range / distance determination**:
- **Contact / near-contact**: stellate wound, soot in wound, muzzle imprint.
- **Close range (<60 cm typical handgun)**: visible GSR + soot patterns on clothing + target.
- **Intermediate (~60-120 cm)**: GSR pattern characterization via SEM-EDS or sodium-rhodizonate testing on target clothing → reproduce by test-firing at measured distances.
- **Long range (>120 cm)**: minimal GSR; rely on trajectory + caliber + wound for indirect inference.

**Gunshot residue** (we covered in trace lesson):
- **Shooter GSR** — SEM-EDS Pb-Sb-Ba spheres on hand, face.
- **Target GSR** — pattern on victim clothing for range determination.
- **Caveats**: secondary transfer, environmental sources (mechanics, fireworks).

**Modern critiques + reform**:
- **NAS 2009** *Strengthening Forensic Science*: criticized firearms / tool-mark identification for lack of empirical error-rate studies; subjective + non-quantified comparison; over-claimed individualization.
- **PCAST 2016** *Forensic Science in Criminal Courts*: applied Daubert; concluded firearm identification has *foundational validity issues* — empirical error-rate studies were limited + ambiguously interpreted. Recommended further research + transparent uncertainty reporting.
- **Recent error-rate studies** (Ames I + II 2014 + 2020; Baldwin et al.): measured ~0.7-1% false-positive rate; ~5-15% inconclusive rate. Substantially higher false-positive risk than DNA.
- **AFTE response**: defended methodology + expanded conclusion-tier guidance; emphasized that examiners report 'identification' only with sufficient individual characteristics; emerging support for **probabilistic / likelihood-ratio framing**.
- **3D virtual comparison microscopy + machine-learning matching** (TopMatch, ALIAS, NIST projects): emerging objective methods; potential to replace or supplement subjective microscopic comparison.
- **Brady disclosure**: examiner training + proficiency-test results + lab QC failures are increasingly disclosed.

**Modern best practice**: comparison-microscope examination + IBIS / NIBIN leads + AFTE methodology + documented + transparent conclusion + appropriate uncertainty + (increasingly) machine-learning + likelihood-ratio reporting. The discipline retains substantial probative value but the *individualization-to-the-exclusion-of-all-others* claim is no longer defensible without empirical foundation.

question.question: Compare a fired bullet to a suspect's firearm
question.goal: A 9mm Luger bullet was recovered at a homicide scene; the suspect's firearm is a Glock 17. Walk through the comparison methodology.

steps.prompt: First, what class characteristics do you determine + how?

acceptedAnswers: caliber + number of lands and grooves + twist direction + twist rate + rifling type (polygonal vs. conventional)

hints: Rifling features visible on the bullet.
steps.reveal: **Class characteristics**: caliber (9mm via bullet weight + diameter), number of lands + grooves (Glock = polygonal hexagonal rifling — distinctive class), direction of twist (Glock = right-hand), twist rate (1:9.84 inches Glock 17). The bullet must show these consistent with the suspect firearm. Inconsistent class (e.g. 6 land + grooves on a Glock-victim bullet) → **elimination at class level**. Polygonal rifling produces softer, more diffuse striae than cut rifling — a known challenge for individual-characteristic comparison.

steps.prompt: How do you produce a comparison standard from the suspect firearm?

acceptedAnswers: test-fire into a water tank or cotton-bale catcher with the same caliber + manufacture of ammunition; recover at least two undeformed bullets

steps.reveal: **Test-firing**: load the suspect firearm with **same caliber + same brand / lot of ammunition** as the evidence (where possible); fire into a **water tank** (most common, preserves bullet without deformation) or **cotton-bale catcher**. Recover at least two test bullets per firearm — to establish the firearm's reproducible striae + to compare test-to-test as an internal consistency check. Also recover **test cartridge cases** for breech-face / firing-pin / ejector / extractor comparison.

steps.prompt: What microscopic features do you align on the comparison microscope?

acceptedAnswers: striae on lands + grooves on bullet; breech-face + firing-pin marks on cartridge case

steps.reveal: **Comparison microscope**: place evidence bullet on one stage, test bullet on the other; rotate to align corresponding land-engraved area; magnify ~30-50×; align striae in the optical bridge — same patterns of microscopic lines = **individualizing match**. For Glock polygonal rifling, the striae are subtler — examiners may need to compare additional features (sub-class characteristics). For cartridge cases: align **breech-face textures** (machined surface marks on the rear of the case) + **firing-pin impressions** (shape + striae of firing-pin tip). Document with photomicrographs.

steps.prompt: What conclusion tier do you report + with what uncertainty?

acceptedAnswers: identification, inconclusive, or elimination; PCAST + Ames studies indicate ~1% false positive; emerging likelihood-ratio reporting

steps.reveal: **Conclusion**: per AFTE — **identification**, **inconclusive**, or **elimination**. PCAST 2016 + Ames I/II studies indicate ~0.7-1% false-positive rate + ~5-15% inconclusive rate; report with uncertainty. Modern reporting increasingly uses **likelihood-ratio framing**: $LR = P(\text{observed striae} | \text{same firearm}) / P(\text{observed striae} | \text{different firearm})$. Independent **verification** by a second examiner (ideally blind to original conclusion). NIBIN entry + IBIS search for further cases.

question.question: What is the role of NIBIN in modern firearms forensic investigation?
options: NIBIN (National Integrated Ballistic Information Network — ATF-operated) is a national database of 3D digital images of bullets + cartridge cases captured by IBIS (Integrated Ballistic Identification System). It produces ranked candidate lists of potential matches across cases + jurisdictions — providing investigative *leads*, not identifications. A NIBIN 'hit' triggers a human firearms examiner to compare the actual physical exhibits under a comparison microscope using AFTE methodology to render an identification, inconclusive, or elimination conclusion. NIBIN has linked tens of thousands of cases across the US, often connecting seemingly unrelated shootings (the same firearm used in multiple crimes), gun-trafficking networks, + gang activity. Analogous to AFIS for fingerprints — database-driven lead generation, examiner-driven final attribution.
question.explanation: NIBIN (ATF-operated) is the US national IBIS database of 3D bullet + cartridge-case images. It generates ranked candidate lists across cases + jurisdictions, providing investigative *leads* — but final identification requires human firearms examiner comparison-microscope analysis using AFTE methodology. Analogous to AFIS for fingerprints; has linked tens of thousands of cases, gun trafficking, + gang activity.

slides.workedSolution: NIBIN is the ATF-operated US national IBIS database. It captures 3D images of bullets + cartridge cases + provides ranked candidate-list leads across cases + jurisdictions. Hits trigger human firearms examiner comparison-microscope analysis using AFTE methodology for final identification. Analogous to AFIS for fingerprints; has linked tens of thousands of cases including gun-trafficking networks.

question.question: Defending an AFTE identification under PCAST
question.prompt: A firearms examiner has reported an 'identification' linking a recovered 9mm bullet to a suspect Glock 17. The defense cites PCAST 2016 + the Ames II study (false-positive rate ~1%) to challenge the testimony. How should the prosecution + examiner present the methodology + uncertainty under modern Daubert + FRE 702 (2023) standards?

question.question: A Glock 17 has a rifling twist rate of 1:9.84 inches. How many full revolutions does a bullet make traveling 17 inches down the barrel? (Round to 2 decimals.)

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain how Goddard's 1929 comparison-microscope methodology evolved into modern IBIS / NIBIN + machine-learning-augmented ballistics + why uncertainty reporting matters today.
question.rubric: Mentions: Goddard + the comparison microscope (Gravelle 1925) + St. Valentine's Day Massacre 1929 — established firearms identification via microscopic striae on bullets + cartridge cases (rifling lands + grooves + breech-face + firing-pin marks). AFTE methodology + conclusion tiers (identification, inconclusive, elimination). IBIS captures 3D digital images + searches the NIBIN national database — ATF-operated; provides ranked leads, not identifications. NAS 2009 + PCAST 2016 critiqued the discipline's lack of empirical error-rate studies; the Ames I + II studies measured ~0.7-1% false-positive rate + 5-15% inconclusive; modern best practice uses transparent uncertainty + emerging likelihood-ratio + 3D virtual comparison + machine learning. The discipline retains probative value but cannot claim individualization-to-exclusion-of-all-others without empirical foundation — FRE 702 (2023) reinforces this.
